concerns.label: Acne & breakouts
concerns.description: Clogged pores, blackheads, whiteheads and inflamed spots.

concerns.label: Dryness & dehydration
concerns.description: Tightness, flaking and a skin barrier that struggles to hold water.

concerns.label: Dark spots & uneven tone
concerns.description: Post-acne marks, sun spots and melasma.

concerns.label: Fine lines & firmness
concerns.description: Loss of elasticity, expression lines and collagen decline.

concerns.label: Redness & sensitivity
concerns.description: Reactive, easily irritated skin, rosacea and visible flushing.

concerns.label: Rough texture
concerns.description: Bumpy, uneven surface and enlarged-looking pores.

concerns.label: Excess oil & shine
concerns.description: Overactive sebum production through the day.

concerns.label: Dullness
concerns.description: Skin that looks tired, grey or lacking radiance.

concerns.label: Damaged barrier
concerns.description: Stinging, over-exfoliation and compromised skin defences.

conflict_rules.title: Retinoid + AHA
conflict_rules.explanation: Both accelerate cell turnover. Layered in the same routine they commonly cause stinging, peeling and a damaged barrier.
conflict_rules.guidance: Alternate nights - retinoid one evening, acid the next. Never in the same application.

conflict_rules.title: Retinoid + BHA
conflict_rules.explanation: Two exfoliating pathways at once. Tolerable for some skin, but a frequent cause of irritation when starting out.
conflict_rules.guidance: Separate into AM and PM, or alternate nights until you know your tolerance.

conflict_rules.title: Retinoid + Benzoyl Peroxide
conflict_rules.explanation: Benzoyl peroxide oxidises and deactivates most retinoids, so you get the irritation of both with the benefit of neither. Adapalene is the exception - it is stable alongside benzoyl peroxide.
conflict_rules.guidance: Use benzoyl peroxide in the morning and your retinoid at night.

conflict_rules.title: L-Ascorbic Acid + AHA
conflict_rules.explanation: Both need a low pH and both sting. Stacking them raises the total acid load on your skin with no added benefit.
conflict_rules.guidance: Vitamin C in the morning, acids at night.

conflict_rules.title: L-Ascorbic Acid + Niacinamide
conflict_rules.explanation: Largely an internet myth - the flushing reaction requires heat and impurities not found in modern formulas. Some people still find the pair tingles.
conflict_rules.guidance: Safe to layer for most people. Separate them only if you notice flushing.

conflict_rules.title: L-Ascorbic Acid + Retinoid
conflict_rules.explanation: Very different optimal pH levels, and together they are a common source of irritation on sensitive skin.
conflict_rules.guidance: Vitamin C in the morning, retinoid at night - which is the ideal schedule for both anyway.

conflict_rules.title: AHA + BHA
conflict_rules.explanation: Many products already blend the two at balanced strengths. Stacking two separate acid products often over-exfoliates.
conflict_rules.guidance: Pick one acid product per session. If both are in a single formula, that is fine as sold.

conflict_rules.title: Benzoyl Peroxide + AHA
conflict_rules.explanation: Both are drying, and together they strip the barrier fast on acne-prone skin that is already compromised.

conflict_rules.title: Benzoyl Peroxide + L-Ascorbic Acid
conflict_rules.explanation: Benzoyl peroxide oxidises vitamin C, degrading it before it can work.
conflict_rules.guidance: Use them at opposite ends of the day, or on alternate days.

allergen_groups.label: Fragrance
allergen_groups.note: Undisclosed scent blends plus the 26 fragrance components the EU requires to be declared by name. Fragrance is the single most common cause of cosmetic contact allergy.

allergen_groups.label: Essential oils
allergen_groups.note: Botanical oils used for scent. Naturally rich in the same terpenes that make fragrance allergenic.

allergen_groups.label: Isothiazolinone preservatives
allergen_groups.note: MI and MCI caused a Europe-wide contact allergy epidemic and are now restricted to rinse-off products.

allergen_groups.label: Formaldehyde releasers
allergen_groups.note: Preservatives that work by slowly releasing formaldehyde. Relevant to anyone patch-test positive for formaldehyde.

allergen_groups.label: Parabens
allergen_groups.note: Preservative family. Genuine paraben allergy is uncommon, but it is one of the most frequently avoided groups.

allergen_groups.label: Sulfates
allergen_groups.note: Strong anionic surfactants. More often an irritant than a true allergen, but a common request.

allergen_groups.label: Lanolin
allergen_groups.note: Wool-derived occlusive. Lanolin alcohol is the fraction responsible for most lanolin allergy.

allergen_groups.label: Nut and seed oils
allergen_groups.note: Tree-nut, peanut and seed derived oils, for anyone managing a nut or seed allergy.

allergen_groups.label: Wheat and oat derivatives
allergen_groups.note: Wheat- and oat-derived ingredients, for coeliac disease or wheat allergy. Topical gluten is not absorbed, but it matters around the mouth and for contact urticaria.

allergen_groups.label: Chemical UV filters
allergen_groups.note: Organic UV filters. Oxybenzone in particular is the leading photoallergen among sunscreen actives.

allergen_groups.label: Classic patch-test allergens
allergen_groups.note: Substances that appear on standard dermatology patch-test panels because they cause allergic contact dermatitis often enough to be worth testing for.
